Its also really dark because, well, humans contain darkness. If you want to follow that darkness, the algorithm fully understands and will give you what you want. Really effectively.

Part of this is really cool, because you can teach the algorithm your natural interests and it will walk you through all the adjacent  communities to see what keeps you interested. More effective than YouTube because the time-to-interest (or lack) is so quick.

Also, the mechanism for diving into a community is completely passive. Just by spending a few more seconds on the video or hitting the share button you guarantee the algorithm will give you more content from that particular community.
The interesting thing about TikTok is the speed through which you can ricochet through subcultures- the same experience on Twitter/FB/IG would require following/unfollowing a huge number of accounts.

RT @OlsenVet: 5 yrs since Oakland cops evicted OO & shot me. Much gratitude to the brave ppl who evacuated me. The struggle goes on... we c…
Oakland taught me who I am. What is important to me. What real community looks like. What it means to fight for what you believe in.
There is so much work to be done. And reflecting on these last 5 years- each year my goals crystallized through those nights in Oakland.
I know this sounds naive but how is it 5 years later and we are still fighting this fight? In that perspective, what progress has been made?
In a lot of ways this is the 5yr anniversary of me realizing that inequality in policing is one of the biggest fights of our generation.
Occupy Oakland was (imo) a proto-#BlackLivesMatter movement. OO taught me about Oscar Grant, Alan Blueford, and of course the FTP marches.
It was also in those moments Occupy Oakland, imo, became more about police violence than about Wall St or the bankers.
It was in those moments that things became crystal clear to me. I realized how big the battle was. I realized the risks. And the importance.
5 years ago tomorrow, instead of celebrating my birthday I remember buying candles and lighting them at Scott Olsen's vigil.
I remember the next day vividly, it was my birthday but it didn't feel like it. I had just woken up to how viciously police treated people.
Everything was chaos. I didn't see it but it was then that Scott Olsen was struck with a tear gas cannister. People helping flashbanged.
I've spent a lot of energy trying to put myself in those situations again. Oakland taught me something about myself that night.
Adrenaline off the charts- explosions of tear gas and flashbangs, people everywhere yelling- but I felt comfortable behind the viewfinder.
As I ran in the direction hundreds of people were running away from, I felt a new feeling, oddly comfortable. It changed my life.
As I was walking around the plaza, I heard a couple of explosions. Tear gas and people running filled the street. I ran towards the sound.
As night fell, people started lining up at the barricades at Frank Ogawa- now re-named Oscar Grant Plaza. People wanted it back.
They shut down the intersection of 14th and Broadway, danced to Michael Jackson at the cops. I had never seen that before. I loved it.
I'd been in protests before in NY and DC. But the energy in Oakland was different. So strong and so angry. But always with a tinge of joy.
I called out sick from work that day- the 12th st BART station was closed anyway IIRC. That afternoon, Oakland marched in response.
That was my first interaction with OPD and it set the tone for every interaction thereafter.
He saw me taking photos- I thought I was safe. I wasn't. He raised his baton over his head, still holding my collar, and told me to gtfo
Walking away from the plaza, I passed a barricaded street (walking by, not towards it) - a cop reached across, grabbing me by the collar
Most of the arrests had already happened- the camp was largely torn to shreds- I watched cops finish the job, ripping apart everything
I'd moved into my Oakland apartment about a month earlier, I didn't really know Oakland or about OPD or it's history. I was naive.
I woke up my roommate and grabbed my camera, went out in the dark to see what was going on, the fog of teargas & cops filled downtown

I keep feeling like there is some piece of essential tooling that I am missing around the management of my "published" photos / screenshots across devices, and realizing the easiest and most reliable right now are Twitter and Instagram https://t.co/ibufQIsrb1

Anyway this part is the hard part- so I end up having gobs of screenshots and photos and half-written blog posts in IA Writer and Day one and never publish any of it because there is so much friction to turn those things into a published post on my site, and I want it to be easy

So on Mobile, I need to figure out some way of converting a Day One export into uploaded Cloudinary images (https://t.co/ApGngK0SpH by @etportis looks like a good lead) and then fixing the inline image URLs based on the uploaded images, then commit that to git somehow and PR https://t.co/uOy1kVaofZ
Day One would be my preferred method of composing posts on mobile. Plus Day One offers some nice export options, but the markdown ones don’t include the image assets. https://t.co/86OYf2Rzzg

Not only that, but how do I make sure that my Markdown document refers to the right Cloudinary URLs without me copying in every single one? I should be able to drag an image into my .md, press publish, and everything is uploaded and hotswapped for me, somehow

On Desktop, I really like IA Writer, which has some basic image handling. If I drag an image into a .md document I am editing, IA Writer will copy the image next to it and include it as a local image reference, which is cool and good. But how to get those to Cloudinary? https://t.co/nECAlqzlKi

My current process involves dragging images into my Cloudinary image library and then, one by one, copying the URLs back into my Markdown post. This works but feels extremely inelegant, and takes a lot of clicks. Doesn't really work well for mobile either. https://t.co/XjRYf18DK7

I write my posts in Markdown, which is awesome because I can compose text and export MD from Day One, or IA Writer – things start to become really complicated when you want to introduce images, though... where do you put them?

I am in no way an expert in community management or how to build a product, but as someone who has a deep love for the value of Twitter, it is baffling to me how little has changed over its lifetime. I get that scale is hard. I get that simplicity is good. But it's malpractice.

"People you should follow" is a joke. Why aren't there better tools for managing who I follow? Why isn't there a tool to unfollow people who haven't tweeted in X years? Or whose tweets I've never liked? Why is the reporting system a black box? Why can't we elect moderators? https://t.co/JYMtee6V96

I know that ideas are cheap and execution is hard, but I believe in you guys. Beyond the abuse issues, there are basic UX wins you could make. @benmschmidt @rbthisted I am taking a long time to say something simple; I much prefer the meta-skill of "Learning Something New" over the specific skill of Computer Science, or even worse, hyper-specific CS like a specific technology or language- gimme the self-driven learner over the expert any day

@benmschmidt @rbthisted I really don't think you need to know how to code anymore. You need to know code *literacy* like for loops, if/then- but most kids get that from playing with redstone in Minecraft when they're 6, and frankly the solutions in the real world not dissimilar

@benmschmidt @rbthisted I mean, it's dramatically changed in the past 6 months for me. I have HS students I am "teaching" basic javascript in combination with a GPT-4 discord bot; they want to do a project, I ask the robot the magic words, and off they go - BUT, that is only possible w/ self-driven kids

@benmschmidt @rbthisted Some of my favorite dataviz practitioners come from other fields, music, science, journalism- and used that existing knowledge to push dataviz further in new directions, new syntheses and approaches;  I would prefer a curious self-driven person with world-knowledge over a "coder"

@benmschmidt @rbthisted I think one of the crucial missing things in this conversation for me isn't CS expertise, it's the ability to be curious and *self-driven* - if you have proven your ability to learn, explore, and create in a new field that's all I need, code is just another medium

@benmschmidt @rbthisted the most successful teams and companies I have seen and been on raise their young, and through doing so make the product better through teaching & access to beginner's mind - and the team benefits from deeply shared experience and learning/growing *together*

@benmschmidt @rbthisted I have seen two different fields (dataviz and AI) emerge before education tracks to support them did- if we are all basically on the same footing, I'd much prefer to learn alongside / train someone junior who has an understanding of the world and how the product fits into it

The world is about to change drastically. Do we break the chains binding us down and share our newly-found technological spoils with everyone equally?

The choice is ours and the time to make it is right now... drown ourselves in filth or spit in the face of colonialism?

Envision neighborhoods joining forces against imbalances caused by technology titans; welcoming open-source AI systems & decision-making tools that uphold our core principles rather than awaiting top-down self-improvement or regulation.

Mutual aid offers hope; fostering cooperation & solidarity can build systems prioritizing well-being over privilege. By focusing on collective good, we can harness AI & crypto power for healing wounds left by centuries-old injustices.

The insatiable greed in our society finds new sustenance in these emerging technologies. We must resist this siren song of commodification if we hope to forge a future driven by equitable use of technology instead of being chained down by the ghosts of capitalism.

Algorithm-led startups commodify labor like colonizers before them. Look at the most recent tech revolutions: crypto and NFTs are created & traded by those with capital - echoing historical control through economic exploitation.

Our AI models are largely constructed from a corpus of white, western perspectives & unleashed upon unsuspecting cultures they were never designed to understand. These puppeteers assume an unquestionable authority while hiding behind their robots.

The seductive allure of these technologies is that they claim to offer a pathway for the oppressed to reclaim economic sovereignty – but in reality, we may be witnessing a 21st Century re-calibration of colonial philosophies.

Traditional colonial systems hoarded knowledge and technology, granting privilege to those deemed worthy. As crypto and AI evolve, they threaten to entrench labor exploitation, resource inequality, and climate injustice in ways that may be difficult to exorcise.

In the digital chaos of the 21st century, we're in danger of entrenching systems of oppression. Crypto and AI promise economic opportunity, but beneath the surface lies a shadow: colonialism re-calibrated for modern times. 🧵👇

@camdez Yeah exactly- the token count doubling is insane. As long as your user prompts are relatively short and your robot answers won't be too long, you could easily stuff hundreds of "memories". The problem is it slows the conversation down a bit as it processes all of that.

@camdez I stuff all of these into the prompt as System-level messages in the format "You remember something important: {memory}" - so to the robot those all appear as system messages that precede the user message.

right now everyone is doing these "close, but" interactions either thru: slot-machine style re-rolling (go back to the drawing board and come back to me) or through a chat-style interface (you made it red, can I have it blue?) but there has to be something better

This is not a problem that computing power or model size can fix; even expert humans struggle to convey their desires to other expert humans when they have extremely overlapping backgrounds and worldviews; conveying to the robot "close, but" will always be part of the UX

Companies that convey the robot as *the solution* to their customers are setting themselves up for resentment by incorrectly framing the power of the tool – companies that allow users to build, monitor, and iterate on boundaries/instructions for the robots quickly will win

If you take this further; the value-add for companies integrating AI into their products is not adding the robot, but knowing when/what to ask the robot, and when to pass up the chain for human intervention, nearly everyone will need to build tooling/UX for this

Right now, the power of the hyper-intelligent robots are as *momentum-builders* - but even the most cutting edge robots can't take you all the way across the finish line. Think of them as extremely powerful firestarters; not firewood

Everyone I talk to wants a Wirecutter for politics. There are some folks that are close but the intelligent news consumer needs to triangulate reality from different sources. Seems like needless overhead to me.

Poll people about what they care about. 

Ask politicians where they stand on those issues. 

Ask experts how they think those policies would affect people. 

Then go back to the people and ask what they care about now. Thats it. Until election day.

There shouldnt be another dollar spent on horserace polling until 

1) We have a full “this is how we fucked up last time” which I have yet to see

2) Wait until a few months before the election, the weather man doesn’t tell you what he thinks the odds are for snow in 6 months

Horserace pollsters have an inherent bias towards volatility- if there is a clear front runner, polls are less interesting week-to-week and are less likely to be commissioned. I wonder about the ways these inherent biases cloud our understanding.

In 1992 they have snazzier graphics overall, but still just a simple state-by-state map. The flag background is timeless. Republicans are still being shown in blue, democrats in red. https://t.co/lP6Zkx29Ux
A small inventory of graphics in NBC's 1984 election broadcast. They have this cool 3D vote bar chart, and a sort of oblong US map. https://t.co/ze2joeGEAo

They "Victory Desk" seems to have now become the "Projection Desk". 

Even fewer maps in this broadcast than in 1960- not even a decorative one in sight (that I could see). Lots of reading numbers that are on the screen. https://t.co/EsjWrEFEwC

Instead of checkmarks for the winners, they put Vs (for Victory!) decided by the NBC Victory Desk (which is the predecessor to what we now call the Decision Desk) https://t.co/bid6DfXckS

The 1960 broadcast begins with an explanation of how NBC counts the votes using "computers". 

"That tape is fed, electronically, into banks of magnetic tape storage reels... Within the computer, tonights returns are compared to 200,00 factors of past elections." https://t.co/AFpXoRSsUk

tweets.text: @ivarvong @simonw Imo its more about closeness and centrality, in the center of your sentences you usually find your higher-level embedding – the smaller ones orbit around it - you could probably make a tree out of it but thats not how my brain thinks about it right now
@ivarvong @simonw Yes, exactly - then the hard part is aggregation and visualizing the aggregations in an intuitive way- my favorite type of problem

@simonw This also allows you some control on how much you “zoom out” when aggregating together related embeddings- the smaller the better lets you find links between clusters and pull a bit from each, or the entire cluster, whatever suits my task
@simonw Ah, I am always clustering / grouping my embeddings- so the smaller the better leads me to the correct cluster, and then that entire cluster is used to inform the rest of the process
@simonw Imo by logical sub-grouping of the data (not random/line-based) if code, then embed each method, if text, each sentence or paragraph, etc- the smaller the better, cost allowing

the bing announcement is fascinating because Microsoft is now piping in realtime search results into their LLM- which is cool, but the average person still can't do it (in Microsoft's vision, they probably never can)
anyway, most of the tools you use every day make it extremely difficult to get the data you want out in plaintext quickly without writing code or spinning up infrastructure right now

so, if I were a founder looking to create the future of LLM-powered AI, I would look to build that piping/glue instead of one-shot products- the person who figures out how to centralize, summarize, and serve personal information to the robot with high user control wins, imo

so basically to unlock the power of LLMs, you need to get good summary data of everything you do in plaintext, essentially piping the output of your various tools (figma layers, to do list items, calendar) to the robot to inform your questions- essentially unix piping

I read the Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace at 14 and it changed my life forever. 

https://t.co/qYSu4XB9Ff
We will create a civilization of the Mind in Cyberspace. May it be more humane and fair than the world your governments have made before.

We must declare our virtual selves immune to your sovereignty, even as we continue to consent to your rule over our bodies. We will spread ourselves across the Planet so that no one can arrest our thoughts.

These increasingly hostile and colonial measures place us in the same position as those previous lovers of freedom and self-determination who had to reject the authorities of distant, uninformed powers.
In our world, whatever the human mind may create can be reproduced and distributed infinitely at no cost. The global conveyance of thought no longer requires your factories to accomplish.

Your increasingly obsolete information industries would perpetuate themselves by proposing laws, in America and elsewhere, that claim to own speech itself throughout the world.

These laws would declare ideas to be another industrial product, no more noble than pig iron.
These may keep out the contagion for a small time, but they will not work in a world that will soon be blanketed in bit-bearing media.
In China, Germany, France, Russia, Singapore, Italy and the United States, you are trying to ward off the virus of liberty by erecting guard posts at the frontiers of Cyberspace.

In our world, all the sentiments and expressions of humanity, from the debasing to the angelic, are parts of a seamless whole, the global conversation of bits. We cannot separate the air that chokes from the air upon which wings beat.
Because you fear them, you entrust your bureaucracies with the parental responsibilities you are too cowardly to confront yourselves.
You are terrified of your own children, since they are natives in a world where you will always be immigrants.

In the United States, you have today created a law, the Telecommunications Reform Act, which repudiates your own Constitution and insults the dreams of Jefferson, Washington, Mill, Madison, DeToqueville, and Brandeis. These dreams must now be born anew in us.

The only law that all our constituent cultures would generally recognize is the Golden Rule. We hope we will be able to build our particular solutions on that basis. But we cannot accept the solutions you are attempting to impose.

Our identities have no bodies, so, unlike you, we cannot obtain order by physical coercion. We believe that from ethics, enlightened self-interest, and the commonweal, our governance will emerge. Our identities may be distributed across many of your jurisdictions.
Your legal concepts of property, expression, identity, movement, and context do not apply to us. They are all based on matter, and there is no matter here.
We are creating a world where anyone, anywhere may express his or her beliefs, no matter how singular, without fear of being coerced into silence or conformity.
We are creating a world that all may enter without privilege or prejudice accorded by race, economic power, military force, or station of birth.
Cyberspace consists of transactions, relationships, and thought itself, arrayed like a standing wave in the web of our communications.
We are forming our own Social Contract. This governance will arise according to the conditions of our world, not yours. Our world is different.

You claim there are problems among us that you need to solve. You use this claim as an excuse to invade our precincts. Many of these problems don't exist. Where there are real conflicts, where there are wrongs, we will identify them and address them by our means.

You have not engaged in our great and gathering conversation, nor did you create the wealth of our marketplaces. You do not know our culture, our ethics, or the unwritten codes that already provide our society more order than could be obtained by any of your impositions.

Cyberspace does not lie within your borders. Do not think that you can build it, as though it were a public construction project. You cannot. It is an act of nature and it grows itself through our collective actions.
Governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. You have neither solicited nor received ours. We did not invite you. You do not know us, nor do you know our world.
You have no moral right to rule us nor do you possess any methods of enforcement we have true reason to fear.

We have no elected government, nor are we likely to have one, so I address you with no greater authority than that with which liberty itself always speaks. I declare the global social space we are building to be naturally independent of the tyrannies you seek to impose on us.
You are not welcome among us. You have no sovereignty where we gather.

@micahstubbs I deleted my Facebook a few months ago and there a photos and videos from friends hidden in there that aren’t accessible any other way. I think that is a profoundly cynical and disturbing state of affairs considering the intent of the technology it is built on top of.

@micahstubbs A “healthy” use of the web would be opening a browser to the latest updates from artists personal sites, distributed and owned by them, curated by an algorithm controlled and understood by me. I want to see a future like that, but we collectively cede control every day.

@micahstubbs I mean, I am old enough to have “gone viral” by being posted on a bunch of blogs consumed through Google Reader. Obviously that couldn’t happen today- but I think the reasons why are a conscious decision by platforms to take more control of the distribution cuz it benefits them.

@micahstubbs I mean, how does HTTP exist? How does D3 exist? Who wrote the specs for RSS, and why? – The foundations were often created without ads & data funding in mind, and were created nonetheless because they were needed.

Maybe the problem is we have been treating our personal websites as output only services. But really, the best websites are two-way. I think we should all be building our own feeds, making our own "algorithms" that we control and understand.

This isn't even anti-facebook, I am truly saddened by how much energy has been spent by incredibly intelligent people to perform these cynical and dishonest scams. Imagine if engineers would work on interesting problems besides selling ads and personal data?

There is no reason that your personal website couldn't ping my personal website when you post an awesome new photo, and yet the entirety of some artists' work is held in an Instagram profile- these are choices we have made as developers, creators, and as a society

To my original point- if I was re-making a social network, it would mostly look like the internet at large, but with the tools of creation and hosting made easier and accessible. Truly accessible, not "gonna make some money off being the middleman" accessible.

The world would be dramatically better if we removed the tech-bro mold that is growing on top of our open protocols, re-selling convenience to users and stripping them of their autonomy and individuality and re-selling their data at every opportunity

The protocols already exist- and the existence of social media in our society reflects a profound failure of people making tools to make websites. I am lucky to own https://t.co/V0RPi2pMUj - how crazy is it that it's standard to host your identity under a corporate TLD?

Twitter was like this for a while- more a protocol than a social network- super easy API, a variety of clients & creators. Then they decided to make money of selling data access and driving up engagement with addictive notifications that aren't available through 3rd parties.
If I could switch all of my Facebook contacts over to a giant mailing list I would do that in a heartbeat- but there are reasons why others wouldn't (even though those reasons are blurry and varied)

If I was going to remake a social network in 2019 to be sustainable and not grow into an anti-user beast, I would make it open-source, super remixable and rebuildable, and based on the simplest and most resilient parts of the web

I have also spent a lot of time refining my interactions with co-pilot, and now my files are structured and commented in a way that lets the robot have enough context to what I am trying to accomplish that it can give me good suggestions, that doubles as easily-readable code too

Getting to that place took years and was a very personal process, and required a lot of soul searching when the technologies that made me work faster were often not the first choices for clients or collaborators, but if you take my tools away I lose my “superpower”

When I start a project now, I do not think about: file naming, file structure, how to get the data, hosting, what libraries to use– what I do think about is: who is this useful for, what will make this easier to understand, how can I add delight and joy— you know, “coding”

Another crucial part of building things quickly is that you are also building the developer experience of the person who has to pick up this prototype and live with it as a product– decisions made for speed often come at the cost of longevity– but it doesn’t have to!

The purpose of this speed for me is to Do More and Learn More, which comes from accelerated failing; prototyping. I want to make more things with more people, and to do that I need to bring the time cost as close to zero as possible, while still using resilient production tech

This probably makes the whole process 1.25x faster, having the right tools that are easy and fast to spin up probably gets me another speed boost, memorizing the names of the incantations within d3 (groups and scales, mostly) saves a bit of time too

With co-pilot this process is a lot less like “coding” and a lot more like directing, in that I arrange a toolset (vue, d3, turf) and data, describe that data in a way a robot can understand, and vaguely gesture at the desired behavior I want, prompting The Robot to code
Truly there is magic in the moments between “that would be cool” and “we have a hosted webapp that can do 80% of that” and I am trying to bring that space down to, like, minutes if I can

How many of the facts being stated have been confirmed? By the author or another reporter? By two sources or 15? Is this a new fact or an old one? What context do I need to understand what is new and why it matters?

If I could be part of whatever it is that journalism turns into on the web, that would be really great, thanks.
I don’t think the big news orgs of yore will grow into the same position on the web. There will be a new, native contender to take that spot
I just think its frustrating to put so much energy into making the old things work in a new environment, instead of trying new things.
What an incredible hard and insurmountable-looking problem: to change how news/journalism is approached and delivered. But we’re all trying.
The internet needs its own newsroom. Or at least one that understands it and can treat it with respect.
I imagine the day when people say “Oh man did you see that story on Guantanamo?” the same way they say “Did you see Sharknado?”
The whole idea of journalism has been warped. I want to start over in the modern age. How many non-blog news orgs have started since 95?
Its a cause/effect problem. News orgs goals are to “get the most eyeballs” instead of be the best / most accurate / most informative source
The problem is that journalists, by-and-large, don’t really make content worth paying for. When they do, the case for why isnt made enough.
Making your news org dependent on Ads is a mistake they are still trying to unravel now. People are happy to pay for good content.
This American Life has set a wonderful model: if you do journalism that is really great, and moving, people will pay to help you do it.
Why is it that no news source really feels “native” to the internet?
I want a 24/hr news site. Not a TV channel. Livestreamers. Tweeters. Longreads. Dataviz. Interviews. Analysis.  No shitty ads. No gimmicks.
I’m kind of sick of seeing smart journos going to old orgs to help them “update” coverage for new era. Stop upgrading dinosaurs. Move on.
Doing the news for the sake of the greater good is important, but no longer the only requirement. Content has to be quality. Delivered well.
No wonder my generation doesn’t give a shit about the news: look at its quality compared to everything else? News needs to be competitive
There is no news source for my generation. Except, kind of, VICE. No one else consistently covers issues I care about, or covers them well.
I just cant help but think that starting fresh would help out a lot. Try new approaches, mediums, without tacking them on to old relics.
From what I can tell the modern way to change the way the news is delivered is to become a billionaire and buy a newsroom, but, y’know…

@amyhoy @stevesi @emollick I'm no whale expert or anything but it's exciting to me to take hours of whalesong; turn it into embeddings; explore the groupings of those embeddings; find the centroids, and then play "ur-songs" back to some whale buddies, and ya know, see what they do- that all makes sense

@amyhoy @stevesi @emollick I don't want to be pedantic- but it's not the same thing, it is the inverse of it; you are saying "the car uses gas to drive, that doesn't mean it understands gas" but you are forgetting that the car built itself, piece by piece, by being shown gas over and over and that's it

@amyhoy @stevesi @emollick I might not be understanding your point correctly- but even if you believe deeply LLMs are stochastic parrots: this is EXACTLY the type of thing you should apply stochastic parrot technology to; language that we do not understand the meaning and shape of

@amyhoy @stevesi @emollick I was responding to the point you made – I disagree strongly that producing plausible-looking strings of words is the only thing LLMs "can do" – the way they build plausible-looking strings of words is derived from the ability to group tokens by meaning without human intervention https://t.co/Ip8BHgbMWY

@amyhoy @stevesi @emollick GPT-3 is unsupervised machine learning; it does not require labeled data or human raters to learn; OpenAI has ALSO done that, but it is not essential to get the LLMs to generate meaningful-looking results (to be very modest) and create meaningful tokens / groupings

@amyhoy @emollick @stevesi what you are describing is an extremely advanced method for linguistic processing and understanding; the exact type of thing that would help these scientists better understand non-human communication - tokenizing whale song would let you analyze and recite "meaningful" patterns https://t.co/IkAKp90FYn

Joy-Driven Development is related to, but not synonymous with the ever-growing concept of "developer experience" – not all DX is joy-driven! And not all joy comes from DX! But often joy-driven development means choosing tools that make building both fun and frictionless

Joy-Driven Development can (and should!) serve as the compass through which your team makes decisions. The goal is not to avoid hard problems, but to make solving hard problems *fun*, and create a better experience both for the team and the end user.
